up.name: Up quark
up.example: Two up and one down valence quarks make a proton.
up.massNote: Running mass at a scale of 2 GeV; not the mass of a free quark.
up.discovery: SLAC: inside the proton, by electron scattering
up.role: The lightest quark. Together with the down quark it builds every proton and neutron, and so, through the energy bound inside them, most of the visible mass around you.
up.origin: Present since the first microseconds after the Big Bang, when the quark–gluon plasma cooled into protons and neutrons. Never observed alone.
up.fate: Stable as the lightest quark. Bound in protons, which have never been seen to decay (lifetime above 10³⁴ years).

down.name: Down quark
down.example: Two down and one up valence quarks make a neutron.
down.massNote: Running mass at a scale of 2 GeV; confinement prevents isolation.
down.discovery: SLAC: inside the proton, by electron scattering
down.role: The up quark's partner. Because it is slightly heavier, the neutron is mainly for that reason slightly heavier than the proton: free neutrons decay while hydrogen is stable, and chemistry as we know it depends on that ordering.
down.origin: In every proton and neutron, since the first microseconds after the Big Bang.
down.fate: In a free neutron a down quark turns into an up quark by emitting a virtual W⁻ (beta decay, about 15 minutes). In stable nuclei that decay would cost energy, so it does not happen.

charm.name: Charm quark
charm.example: Charm and anticharm form the J/ψ meson.
charm.massNote: Running mass evaluated at its own mass scale.
charm.discovery: Brookhaven and SLAC: in the J/ψ
charm.role: Second-generation partner of the strange quark. It was predicted in 1970 to explain why certain kaon decays are almost absent, and its discovery in 1974 convinced physicists that quarks are real.
charm.origin: Not present in ordinary matter. Made in c c̄ pairs whenever a collision has more than about 3 GeV available: in colliders, in cosmic-ray showers, and in the hot early universe.
charm.fate: Decays through the weak force, mostly into a strange quark, in roughly 10⁻¹³ to 10⁻¹² s inside D mesons.

strange.name: Strange quark
strange.example: Strange quarks appear in kaons and strange baryons.
strange.massNote: Running mass at a scale of 2 GeV.
strange.discovery: Manchester: in kaons ("V particles"); understood as a quark in 1964
strange.role: The lightest second-generation quark. “Strange” particles puzzled physicists in 1947: made quickly, in pairs, by the strong force, they decay slowly, one by one, through the weak force. Kaons revealed CP violation in 1964.
strange.origin: Made in s s̄ pairs in collisions above about 1 GeV; cosmic rays produce kaons in the atmosphere.
strange.fate: Decays through the weak force into an up quark, typically in 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻⁸ s inside kaons and hyperons.

top.name: Top quark
top.example: Decays predominantly to a W boson and a bottom quark before forming hadrons.
top.massNote: Rounded direct-reconstruction mass; different mass definitions must not be mixed at high precision.
top.role: The heaviest known elementary particle, roughly the mass of a tungsten atom. Its Higgs coupling is close to 1, the strongest of all, so it dominates Higgs production at the LHC and, with the Higgs mass, decides how stable the vacuum is. It completed the third generation predicted after the bottom quark.
top.origin: Only in high-energy collisions: first made at the Fermilab Tevatron in 1995, now by the millions at the LHC. A t t̄ pair needs at least about 345 GeV.
top.fate: Decays in about 5 × 10⁻²⁵ s, almost always into a bottom quark and a W boson: faster than hadrons can form, so it is the only quark observed “bare”.

bottom.name: Bottom quark
bottom.example: Bottom hadrons produce displaced decay vertices in detectors.
bottom.massNote: Running mass evaluated at its own mass scale.
bottom.role: Third-generation partner of the top. Its discovery in 1977 implied a top quark. B mesons are the main laboratory for matter–antimatter differences among quarks.
bottom.origin: Made in b b̄ pairs above about 10 GeV; the Υ meson (b b̄) was found at Fermilab in 1977.
bottom.fate: Weak decay, mainly into a charm quark, in about 1.5 × 10⁻¹² s: long enough to fly a few millimetres, which gives the displaced vertices used to tag it.

electron.name: Electron
electron.example: Atomic electrons form shells and chemical bonds; moving electrons carry electric current.
electron.massNote: Rest mass, independent of its speed. An electron is elementary; a proton is composite.
electron.role: The lightest charged particle. Nothing lighter carries its charge, so it cannot decay. It builds atomic shells and therefore all of chemistry, electricity, and the emission of light.
electron.origin: Made in the early universe and in beta decays; also created with positrons (pair production) when a gamma ray above 1.022 MeV passes near a nucleus.
electron.fate: Stable: experiments find a lifetime above 10²⁸ years.

muon.name: Muon
muon.example: Cosmic-ray muons reach the ground and often traverse an entire collider detector.
muon.massNote: About 207 electron masses; mean lifetime approximately 2.2 μs.
muon.role: A heavier copy of the electron: same charge and interactions, 207 times the mass. Unpredicted, it was the first sign that nature repeats its particles in generations. Today it is a precision probe (muon g − 2) and a practical tool (muon imaging of volcanoes and pyramids).
muon.origin: Made continually in the upper atmosphere: cosmic-ray protons create pions, which decay into muons. About one muon crosses each square centimetre of ground per minute.
muon.fate: Decays in 2.2 μs (at rest) into an electron and two neutrinos. Atmospheric muons reach the ground only because relativistic time dilation stretches their lives.

tau.name: Tau
tau.example: Produces electrons, muons, or hadrons in its weak decays.
tau.role: The heaviest charged lepton and first member of the third generation (1975). It signalled that a whole third generation should exist.
tau.origin: Made in τ⁺τ⁻ pairs above 3.55 GeV; found at SLAC's SPEAR collider through events with just one electron, one muon, and missing energy.
tau.fate: Decays in about 2.9 × 10⁻¹³ s into a lighter lepton plus neutrinos, or into hadrons: the only lepton heavy enough to do so.

e_neutrino.name: Electron neutrino
e_neutrino.example: Produced in solar fusion and electron-flavor weak interactions.
e_neutrino.massNote: νₑ is a superposition of mass states ν₁, ν₂, ν₃. Oscillations measure mass-squared differences, not one mass for each flavor.
e_neutrino.role: Proposed by Pauli in 1930 to save energy conservation in beta decay. Electron neutrinos carry energy out of the fusion reactions that power the Sun, and their small, nonzero masses point beyond the Standard Model.
e_neutrino.origin: Beta decays and nuclear reactors; the Sun sends about 6 × 10¹⁰ per square centimetre per second to Earth. Relic neutrinos from the Big Bang fill space.
e_neutrino.fate: Stable as far as we know, but it changes flavor while travelling (oscillation), because it is a mixture of mass states.

mu_neutrino.name: Muon neutrino
mu_neutrino.example: Produced with muons in charged-pion decays.
mu_neutrino.massNote: Flavor and mass states differ. At least two neutrino mass states have nonzero mass; the lightest could be massless.
mu_neutrino.role: Its discovery in 1962 proved that neutrinos come in distinct flavors: neutrinos from pion decay make muons, not electrons. This established the lepton generations.
mu_neutrino.origin: Pion and kaon decays: in cosmic-ray showers in the atmosphere and in accelerator neutrino beams.
mu_neutrino.fate: Oscillates into other flavors over long distances; in 1998 Super-Kamiokande's atmospheric-neutrino result first showed that neutrinos have mass.

tau_neutrino.name: Tau neutrino
tau_neutrino.example: Identified through interactions that produce tau leptons when enough energy is available.
tau_neutrino.massNote: There is no separate measured rest mass to assign to the tau flavor. Neutrino mass generation requires physics beyond the minimal Standard Model.
tau_neutrino.role: The last lepton of the third generation; its direct observation in 2000 (DONuT) completed the table of fermions.
tau_neutrino.origin: Decays of tau leptons and of charmed-strange Dₛ mesons made by high-energy proton beams; also from oscillating muon neutrinos.
tau_neutrino.fate: Stable as far as we know; it oscillates among flavors.

photon.name: Photon
photon.example: Visible light, radio waves, and X-rays consist of photons. Photons mediate electromagnetic interactions.
photon.massNote: Zero rest mass does not mean zero energy: E = hf = pc. No rest frame exists for a photon.
photon.role: Carrier of the electromagnetic force: it binds electrons to nuclei and atoms into molecules, and it is light and all electromagnetic radiation. Its zero mass gives the force an unlimited range.
photon.origin: Emitted whenever charged particles accelerate or change energy level, and created by annihilation (e⁻ + e⁺ → γ + γ). The cosmic microwave background holds about 400 photons per cubic centimetre.
photon.fate: Stable; absorbed when it hands its energy to charged matter.

gluon.name: Gluon
gluon.example: Eight color states mediate the strong interaction; gluons also interact with other gluons.
gluon.massNote: Massless but confined: hadronization produces jets rather than isolated gluons.
gluon.role: Carrier of the strong force between quarks. Gluons carry color themselves and therefore attract each other, which produces confinement and most of the mass of protons and neutrons.
gluon.origin: Exchanged constantly inside every hadron; emitted as an extra jet in high-energy collisions, first seen in three-jet events at DESY's PETRA in 1979.
gluon.fate: Never free: within about 10⁻²³ s it turns into a jet of hadrons.

w_boson.name: W boson
w_boson.example: W⁺ and W⁻ mediate charged-current weak processes, including beta decay.
w_boson.massNote: Its large mass helps set the short range of the weak interaction. W bosons also couple to the Higgs field.
w_boson.role: Carrier of the charged weak force, the only interaction that changes one type of quark or lepton into another (d → u in beta decay, and the first step of hydrogen fusion in the Sun). Without it, the heavier generations could not decay.
w_boson.origin: Exchanged virtually in every beta decay; produced as a real particle only above 80 GeV, first at CERN's SppS collider in 1983.
w_boson.fate: Decays in about 3 × 10⁻²⁵ s into a charged lepton and a neutrino, or into a quark–antiquark pair (jets).

z_boson.name: Z boson
z_boson.example: Mediates neutral-current weak scattering, including neutrino scattering without producing a charged lepton.
z_boson.massNote: Electrically neutral but not non-interacting; couples to the Higgs field and weak currents.
z_boson.role: Carrier of the neutral weak force; its discovery confirmed the unification of the electromagnetic and weak interactions. Measuring how quickly it decays showed that there are exactly three light neutrino types.
z_boson.origin: Produced as a real particle above 91 GeV; LEP made about 17 million Z bosons between 1989 and 2000.
z_boson.fate: Decays in about 3 × 10⁻²⁵ s into a fermion–antifermion pair: electrons, muons, taus, quark jets, or invisible neutrinos.

higgs.name: Higgs boson
higgs.example: The observed excitation of the Higgs field; reconstructed from its decay products.
higgs.massNote: A scalar boson, not a gauge force carrier. Its own mass comes from the Higgs potential; photon/gluon couplings occur through loops.
higgs.role: The excitation of the Higgs field, which gives the W and Z bosons their masses and, through Yukawa couplings, the quarks and charged leptons theirs. Without it electrons would be massless and atoms as we know them could not form.
higgs.origin: Made only in high-energy collisions, mainly by gluon fusion through a top-quark loop at the LHC; discovered by ATLAS and CMS in 2012.
higgs.fate: Decays in about 1.6 × 10⁻²² s, most often into b b̄; the rarer γγ and four-lepton decays gave the cleanest discovery signals.

explanation.fermionPair: Neutral-current Z exchange connects the fermions. Charged pairs also exchange photons and can exchange a Higgs; two quarks can exchange gluons.
explanation.compton: Compton-type scattering uses the photon coupling to the charged fermion. The photon itself does not need electric charge.
explanation.quarkGluon: Quark–gluon scattering uses color couplings, including gluon self-interactions. Observable outgoing states hadronize into jets.
explanation.fermionVector: Electroweak vertices allow fermion–vector-boson scattering. Massive charged fermions also admit Higgs exchange; a charged fermion and W can exchange a photon.
explanation.yukawa: The fermion Yukawa coupling permits Higgs–fermion scattering. Its coupling scales with the fermion mass; a listed channel need not be large.
explanation.gluonGluon: Gluons carry color and have three- and four-gluon vertices, so they scatter already at tree level.
explanation.photonW: The W is electrically charged. Photon–W scattering has charged-vector exchange and a contact vertex.
explanation.zz: Higgs exchange supplies tree-level Z–Z scattering. There is no elementary three-Z or four-Z gauge vertex.
explanation.higgsHiggs: The Higgs potential contains cubic and quartic self-couplings, allowing Higgs–Higgs scattering.
explanation.gaugeHiggs: Gauge–Higgs vertices and, where listed, gauge exchange/contact vertices permit scattering. The H label includes couplings of W/Z to the Higgs sector.
explanation.lightByLight: Light-by-light elastic scattering has no tree-level photon self-coupling. Virtual charged-particle loops allow it; it is not forbidden.
explanation.higherOrder: No tree-level elastic route is present in this approximation. Higher-order diagrams can connect the particles through virtual states; their size and leading order depend on the pair and energy.

beta.label: Free-neutron beta decay · weak
beta.explanation: A down valence quark changes into an up quark through a virtual W⁻. The electron and antineutrino share the released energy; the proton recoils. A bound neutron can be stable if nuclear energy balance prevents decay.

annihilation.label: Annihilation · electromagnetic
annihilation.explanation: An electron and positron can turn into two photons. Rest energy becomes photon energy while total energy and momentum remain conserved. The positron has the electron mass and the opposite electric charge.

higgs.label: Higgs decay · loop-induced
higgs.explanation: The Higgs can decay to two photons through charged-particle loops, despite the photon having no direct mass-generating Higgs coupling. Photon pairs help reconstruct the Higgs mass.

forbidden.label: Forbidden · electric charge would change
forbidden.explanation: Charge conservation rules this out: −1 cannot become 0. Passing a charge check alone would still not prove a reaction is possible; energy, momentum, angular momentum, and the available couplings also matter.

electron.name: Electron
electron.why: A charged track matched to an electromagnetic shower is a typical electron signature.

photon.name: Photon
photon.why: A photon is neutral and usually starts a shower in the electromagnetic calorimeter. Conversion to an electron–positron pair in tracker material is an important exception.

muon.name: Muon
muon.why: A penetrating track connects the inner tracker to outer muon chambers.

hadron.name: Charged hadron
hadron.why: A pion or proton is composite. Quarks and gluons hadronize, so experiments reconstruct jets of hadrons rather than free quarks.

neutrino.name: Neutrino
neutrino.why: Usually escapes a collider detector. Missing transverse momentum is inferred from the measured imbalance; it can also arise from other invisible particles or measurement errors.

atom.name: Atom
atom.inside: A tiny nucleus surrounded by electrons, spread out as a quantum cloud. The electrons are elementary; the nucleus is not.
atom.glue: Electromagnetic attraction between the positive nucleus and the negative electrons, carried by photons.
atom.breakIt: A few eV: 13.6 eV ionizes hydrogen. Flames, ultraviolet light, and sparks do it every day; this is the energy scale of chemistry.
atom.evidence: Thomson found the electron in 1897; Rutherford's 1911 gold-foil experiment showed that almost all the mass sits in a nucleus about 100 000 times smaller than the atom.
atom.takeaway: By volume an atom is mostly empty, yet about 99.95% of its mass is in the nucleus.

nucleus.name: Nucleus
nucleus.inside: Protons (charge +1) and neutrons (charge 0), together called nucleons. The number of protons fixes the element; the number of neutrons, the isotope.
nucleus.glue: The residual strong force: the color force between quarks leaks out of color-neutral nucleons, a little like the van der Waals attraction between neutral molecules. It is described as pion exchange and reaches only about 1–3 fm.
nucleus.breakIt: Millions of eV: about 8 MeV per nucleon in typical nuclei, 28.3 MeV to take helium-4 completely apart. Radioactivity, fission, and fusion work on this scale, about a million times the energy of chemistry.
nucleus.evidence: Rutherford identified the proton in 1919, and Chadwick found the neutron in 1932.
nucleus.takeaway: Nuclear energy is about a million times chemical energy because the binding force is much stronger and much shorter-ranged.

nucleon.name: Proton / neutron
nucleon.inside: Three valence quarks (uud for the proton, udd for the neutron) plus a constantly changing “sea” of gluons and quark–antiquark pairs.
nucleon.glue: The strong force, carried by gluons between color charges. It does not weaken with distance; pulling quarks apart creates new quark–antiquark pairs instead (confinement).
nucleon.breakIt: It cannot be broken into free quarks. Hitting a proton with about 140 MeV or more creates pions; much harder hits produce jets of hadrons. What comes out is new hadrons, never loose quarks.
nucleon.evidence: Electron scattering at SLAC in 1968 (Friedman, Kendall, Taylor) revealed point-like scatterers inside the proton, later identified as quarks and gluons.
nucleon.takeaway: The quarks' rest masses make up only about 1% of the proton's mass; the rest is energy of motion and fields.

elementary.name: Quarks and electrons
elementary.inside: Nothing that we can detect. Elementary particles behave as points in every collision measured so far.
elementary.glue: Nothing to hold: without parts, they are excitations of quantum fields.
elementary.breakIt: Not possible, as far as anyone knows. Enough energy creates new particles instead of revealing pieces.
elementary.evidence: LHC collisions at 13.6 TeV probe distances near 10⁻¹⁹ m, about 10 000 times smaller than a proton, and find no structure inside quarks or leptons.
elementary.takeaway: “Elementary” is an experimental statement: no structure found down to the smallest distances probed so far, not a proof that none exists.

hydrogen.name: Hydrogen atom
hydrogen.note: One proton and one electron held by electric attraction. Ionizing it takes 13.6 eV, which ultraviolet light can supply; that is why its mass defect is only about one part in 70 million.

helium4.name: Helium-4 nucleus (alpha particle)
helium4.note: Two protons and two neutrons held by the residual strong force, which overpowers the protons' electric repulsion below about 2 fm. When the Sun fuses hydrogen into helium it releases about 26.7 MeV per nucleus, a little less than 28.3 MeV because two protons must first become neutrons.

proton.name: Proton
proton.lifetime: Stable (no decay seen; lifetime above 10³⁴ years)
proton.note: The three quarks' rest masses add up to only about 9 MeV/c²; nearly all of the proton's 938 MeV/c² comes from the quarks' motion and the energy of the gluon field that confines them: E = mc² read backwards.

neutron.name: Neutron
neutron.lifetime: About 879 s (15 minutes) when free; stable inside most nuclei
neutron.note: Slightly heavier than the proton (by 1.29 MeV/c²), so a free neutron decays: n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. Inside a stable nucleus that decay would cost energy, so it does not happen.

lambda.name: Lambda baryon
lambda.note: A proton-like baryon with a strange quark in place of a down quark. The strong force makes it together with a kaon (strangeness comes in pairs), but it can decay only through the weak force (Λ → p + π⁻), hence its “strangely” long life.

omega.name: Omega-minus baryon
omega.note: Three strange quarks. Gell-Mann's quark pattern predicted its charge, strangeness, and mass before it was seen at Brookhaven in 1964, the decisive test of the quark model. Three identical quarks in one state also required a new quantum number: color.

pion.name: Positive pion
pion.note: Predicted by Yukawa in 1935 as the carrier of the nuclear force. As the lightest hadron it sets the force's range, about 1.4 fm. Its decay into μ⁺ + νμ is the main source of cosmic-ray muons.

kaon.name: Positive kaon
kaon.note: The lightest strange meson. Neutral kaons showed in 1964 that nature slightly distinguishes matter from antimatter (CP violation).

dmeson.name: Neutral D meson
dmeson.note: A charm quark with an anti-up quark: charm that is not cancelled by anticharm. Its weak decays, usually into kaons, confirmed “open charm” in 1976.

jpsi.name: J/psi meson
jpsi.note: Charm and anticharm, discovered in 1974 at Brookhaven (J) and SLAC (ψ) at the same time. It is lighter than a pair of D mesons, so it cannot simply fall apart into them, and it lives about a thousand times longer than typical hadrons of its mass. This “November Revolution” established the charm quark.

bmeson.name: Positive B meson
bmeson.note: An up quark with an anti-bottom quark. It flies a few millimetres in a detector before decaying, which lets experiments tag bottom quarks, and it is the main system for measuring matter–antimatter differences among quarks.

upsilon.name: Upsilon meson
upsilon.note: Bottom and antibottom, seen at Fermilab in 1977 as a bump in muon pairs. Here the quark masses supply most of the total: heavy quarks move slowly, so field energy is a smaller share than in a proton.

electronPair.label: Electron–positron pair
electronPair.first: Anderson saw positrons in cosmic rays in 1932, a year after Dirac predicted antimatter. A gamma ray above 1.022 MeV passing near a nucleus routinely makes such pairs.
electronPair.fate: Both are stable. The positron soon meets an electron and annihilates into two 511 keV photons, the signal used in PET medical scans.

muonPair.label: Muon–antimuon pair
muonPair.first: Muons were found in cosmic rays in 1936 (Anderson and Neddermeyer), made by pion decays rather than in pairs. Electron–positron colliders make μ⁺μ⁻ pairs directly.
muonPair.fate: Each muon decays after about 2.2 μs (at rest) into an electron and two neutrinos.

pionPair.label: Pion pair (up and down quarks)
pionPair.first: Charged pions were found in cosmic rays in 1947 by Powell's group and produced at Berkeley's cyclotron in 1948.
pionPair.fate: Charged pions decay in 26 ns into a muon and a neutrino; this is how cosmic rays make muons.

kaonPair.label: Kaon pair (strange quarks)
kaonPair.first: Kaons appeared in cosmic-ray cloud-chamber photographs in 1947 (Rochester and Butler) as “V particles”. The strong force always makes strange quarks together with strange antiquarks.
kaonPair.fate: Kaons decay through the weak force after about 10 ns, often into a muon and a neutrino.

protonPair.label: Proton–antiproton pair
protonPair.first: The antiproton was made in 1955 at Berkeley's Bevatron, an accelerator built with just enough energy for p + p → p + p + p + p̄.
protonPair.fate: Each is stable on its own, but the antiproton annihilates as soon as it meets ordinary matter, typically into several pions.

charm.label: Charm–anticharm (J/ψ)
charm.first: Discovered in November 1974 at the same time at SLAC's SPEAR electron–positron collider and at Brookhaven (a proton beam on beryllium).
charm.fate: The J/ψ lives about 7 × 10⁻²¹ s and decays into hadrons or, about 12% of the time, into an electron or muon pair.

tauPair.label: Tau–antitau pair
tauPair.first: Martin Perl's group found the tau at SPEAR in 1975 through puzzling events with just one electron, one muon, and missing energy.
tauPair.fate: Each tau decays in about 0.3 ps, for example τ⁻ → μ⁻ + ν̄μ + ντ; the neutrinos explain the missing energy.

bottom.label: Bottom–antibottom (Υ)
bottom.first: The Υ was observed in 1977 at Fermilab by Leon Lederman's experiment, as a peak in muon pairs from proton–nucleus collisions near 9.5 GeV.
bottom.fate: The Υ decays in about 10⁻²⁰ s; heavier b b̄ pairs separate into B mesons that live about 1.5 ps.

zBoson.label: Z boson
zBoson.first: First seen in 1983 at CERN's SppS proton–antiproton collider (UA1, UA2). LEP (1989–2000) then produced millions by tuning electron–positron collisions to 91.2 GeV.
zBoson.fate: Decays in about 3 × 10⁻²⁵ s into a fermion–antifermion pair; about 20% of the time into invisible neutrinos.

wPair.label: W⁺W⁻ pair
wPair.first: Single W bosons were found in 1983 at CERN's SppS. LEP's higher-energy phase (LEP2, from 1996) produced W pairs and measured how they couple to each other.
wPair.fate: Each W decays in about 3 × 10⁻²⁵ s into a charged lepton plus a neutrino, or into two quark jets.

higgs.label: Higgs boson (with a Z)
higgs.first: LEP's maximum of 209 GeV fell just short of the 216 GeV needed for Z + H. The Higgs was discovered at the LHC in 2012, mostly produced by gluon fusion.
higgs.fate: Decays in about 1.6 × 10⁻²² s, most often into b b̄; the rare γγ and four-lepton decays gave the cleanest discovery signals.

topPair.label: Top–antitop pair
topPair.first: No electron–positron collider has reached 345 GeV yet. Top quarks were discovered in 1995 at Fermilab's Tevatron in proton–antiproton collisions (CDF and DØ).
topPair.fate: Each top decays in about 5 × 10⁻²⁵ s into a bottom quark and a W boson, before it can form a hadron.
